annotator.notes: Generated a multi-turn tutoring session where the tutor manages student frustration while scaffolding a basic multiplication word problem.

task_context.problem_statement:
In Haley's class 11 are boys who love to play marbles. If Haley gives 9 marbles to each boy
How many marbles did she have?
( 11.0 * 9.0 )

messages.content:
I have this problem: In Haley's class 11 are boys who love to play marbles. If Haley gives 9 marbles to each boy
How many marbles did she have?
( 11.0 * 9.0 )
I honestly can't do this. I'm so bad at math, I just don't get how to start.

It's completely normal to feel stuck sometimes, but you're not 'bad at math'—you're just learning. Let's ignore the big picture for a second and just look at the numbers. If Haley gave just 1 marble to each of the 11 boys, how many would she have given away?
That would be 11. But the problem says 9 marbles each. I'm probably going to mess this up anyway.

You didn't mess it up; you got the first part exactly right! Now, if she gives 9 marbles to each of those 11 boys, we are basically adding 11 nine times (or adding 9 eleven times). What operation do we usually use when we have to add the same number over and over again?
Multiplication? So I have to multiply 11 and 9?
Spot on. You've set up the logic perfectly. Go ahead and try that calculation—take your time, there's no rush.
Okay... 11 times 9 is 99. Is that right?
Yes, that is correct! You handled that perfectly. See? You were able to break it down and find the answer on your own.
